problem: Video-LLM-based VLN agents (NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NaVILA, MapNav) do not scale well to long video streams. Sampling a fixed number of frames loses the fine temporal resolution needed for low-level actions. Pooling or merging tokens into sparse memory loses visual and temporal detail. Most of these methods also refresh the whole LLM dialogue context at every step, so all history is prefilled again each turn and latency and compute grow with episode length.
motivation: Real-world VLN needs an agent that processes a continuous camera stream and acts with low, stable latency while still keeping long-horizon context. Reusing the KV cache across dialogue turns can remove over 99% of prefill time. However, the KV cache grows linearly (about 5 GB per 2K tokens), and Video-LLMs reason worse over very long contexts. Feature-level compression such as average pooling also prevents reusing already-computed KV states.
key_idea: Treat navigation as a streaming multi-turn dialogue with a Video-LLM. A fast sliding window of the last N dialogue turns keeps its KV cache for responsive action decoding. A slow-updating memory keeps a fixed number of temporally sampled past frames, whose tokens are further pruned at test time by 3D voxel de-duplication, so context size and latency stay bounded.
insight: A bounded, fixed-size memory generalizes better than full history. With a window of 8, memory of 8×196 tokens reaches 45.5 SR, versus 40.0 when the entire visual context is used and 37.3 with 2×196 (Table 4). The authors attribute this to long, variable-length contexts biasing training. Pruning redundant tokens rather than compressing features keeps KV states reusable and the Video-LLM's pretrained representations intact: test-time voxel pruning removes about 20% of tokens yet adds +1.2 SR on R2R-CE and +1.1 SR on RxR-CE (Table 6), while pruning during training hurts. Most of the performance comes from data. DAgger adds +5.5 SR, RxR data +7.8 SR, VideoQA+MMC4 co-training +5.3 SR, MMC4 interleaved data a further +2.0 SR, and a 150K-trajectory ScaleVLN subset +2.9 SR (Table 5).
method: Interleaved VLA dialogue on LLaVA-Video-7B (Qwen2-7B): each episode is a multi-turn dialogue. Each user turn carries the current RGB frame; the assistant replies with 4 low-level actions encoded as single rare-symbol tokens (↑ = forward 25 cm, ←/→ = turn 15°, plus STOP). A session has 8 turns, i.e. 32 actions.

Fast-streaming dialogue context: a sliding-window KV cache over the last N=8 turns is kept and reused, so only the new observation tokens are prefilled. When the window fills, its KV states are offloaded; prompt and action token states are discarded and observation states move to memory.

Slow-updating memory context: past windows are summarized by uniformly sampling a fixed number of frames (8, following NaVILA; 196 tokens each). The decoder attends to the current observation, the memory tokens {M_0..M_j} and the current window's KV cache.

Voxel-based spatial pruning (test time only): image patches are back-projected into shared 3D using depth and voxelized. Within each temporal stride K, only the most recent token per voxel is kept, and frames retaining fewer than a θ fraction of their tokens are dropped entirely. This prunes about 20% of tokens without recomputing earlier KV states.

Two-stage training with DAgger: stage 1 trains for one epoch on oracle trajectories. Stage 2 collects 240K DAgger corrective samples, using Habitat's shortest-path follower as expert, and trains one more epoch.

Multi-source co-training: VLN data (450K clips from R2R, EnvDrop and RxR in 60 MP3D scenes, plus 300K ScaleVLN HM3D samples) is mixed with 248K VideoQA samples (LLaVA-Video-178K, ScanQA) and 230K MMC4 interleaved image-text samples to preserve general reasoning.

setting.training_data: 450K VLN video clips from R2R, R2R-EnvDrop and RxR (60 MP3D scenes, Habitat); +300K samples from a ScaleVLN subset (~150K trajectories, 700 HM3D scenes) for the † model; 240K DAgger samples; 248K VideoQA (LLaVA-Video-178K + ScanQA); 230K MMC4 interleaved image-text. ~1500 A100 GPU hours.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB stream (depth, and implicitly camera pose, used only for test-time voxel pruning); RealSense D455 RGB-D on the real robot
setting.action_space: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT/RIGHT 15° / STOP, 4 actions per dialogue turn
setting.privileged: none (depth and pose used for voxel pruning come from the agent's sensors)

results: StreamVLN† reaches 56.9 SR / 51.9 SPL on R2R-CE val-unseen and 52.9 SR / 46.0 SPL / 61.9 nDTW on RxR-CE val-unseen. These are the best reported among RGB-only methods, beating NaVILA† (54.0 / 49.0 on R2R-CE; 49.3 / 44.0 on RxR-CE) and Uni-NaVid† (47.0 / 42.7). It roughly matches panoramic, waypoint-based ETPNav (57.0 / 49.0) and exceeds ScaleVLN-HAMT (55.0 / 51.0) while using only 150K of ScaleVLN's 3M trajectories. Without extra data it still leads RGB-only methods at 52.8 SR / 47.2 SPL on R2R-CE. It also reaches 35.8 SR on HM3D ObjectNav without ObjectNav training, above NaVid (32.5) and MapNav (34.6) but below modular zero-shot VoroNav (42.0). Latency stays stable at about 0.27 s per 4 actions thanks to KV-cache reuse.
limitations: Generating low-level actions directly from raw RGB is less robust to viewpoint changes and occlusion, which can give suboptimal real-world control.
The hybrid context strategy still struggles with very long-horizon navigation, and there is no quantitative real-world evaluation (qualitative demos only).
Keeping explicit action history in the dialogue complicates asynchronous inference and deployment, since past actions must be synchronized. Voxel pruning additionally requires depth and pose.
